rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1, 3.1 and 3.3 - the authors deployed their own IoT monitoring system (TEROS 12 soil sensors, two Davis weather stations, ESP32/GSM nodes) in eight drip-irrigated olive parcels in eastern Crete during 2021-2022, collected real-time soil moisture, EC, temperature and weather data, and compared the platform's weekly irrigation dose and fruit-fly alarms with manually calculated FAO-56 values for the 2022 irrigation season.
rows.notes: The technology matches (an IoT platform that computes weekly irrigation dose per tree from FAO-56 Penman and 30 cm soil moisture and e-mails the farmer), but the study reports no result of its own on water conservation or water-use efficiency. The only evaluation (Section 3.3) is that the platform's recommended dose equals the manually calculated FAO-56 dose for all parcels, i.e. a check that the calculation works, not a measurement of water applied, water saved, yield or water productivity. Statements that the system 'ensures water saving' or 'can contribute to increased water-use efficiency' are assertions, not findings. The study therefore supports only the precondition (the platform calculates and delivers irrigation requirements), not the claimed effect of efficient water use. Limitations stated (preliminary user testing, single crop/region, future automation) concern the system, not a water-conservation result; no dispersion statistics on any outcome are reported.

notes: Full text appears complete though with some duplicated/overlapping lines from the PDF layout. The paper is primarily a system design and implementation description; no field experiment comparing water use with and without the platform was conducted.
